item.title: The Calling of Saint Matthew
item.museum: Contarelli Chapel, San Luigi dei Francesi, Rome
item.lesson: Caravaggio's first great public commission changed painting overnight. The Gospel scene — Christ calling the tax collector Matthew to follow him — is staged not in holy antiquity but in what looks like a dim Roman tavern, with Matthew's crew dressed in the flashy street fashion of Caravaggio's own day, counting the take. Christ enters at right, nearly swallowed by shadow, and points; a blade of light cuts across the wall above him and lands on the men at the table. That raking light against darkness — tenebrism — became the Baroque's signature special effect, copied from Naples to Amsterdam. Caravaggio himself lived like one of his paintings: brawls, arrests, and eventually a killing that sent him fleeing Rome for the rest of his short life. The gesture of Christ's hand deliberately echoes Adam's on the Sistine ceiling: a new creation beginning in a back room.
item.lookFor: Follow the pointing hands — Christ points, Peter points, the bearded man points down the table — and notice the painting never quite settles which man is Matthew. Scholars still argue about it.
